Row.Text: As Gilgamesh’s court grows, so do its duties, and so does its drudgery. The great king paces the stone floors like a bull – head held high, railing at his subjects, and flying into fits of rage. Something must be done.
New horizons, new faces, new experiences distract from the dullness of home.
Gilgamesh has seen the world, uncovered its secrets… and yet still yearns for a foe worthy of his might. Or, perhaps, a friend.
The drums of war, the clash of bronze call.
Under a hail of arrows, soaked in fear-sweat - this is where friendships are forged.
Use the Levy Unit action on a City-State.
The stylus and clay tablet, the hush of the library call.
Gilgamesh loves a contest. He wrestles with his generals, he plays the game of Ur with his scribes. But he yearns for a friend who is his equal – or equal to his opinion of himself – in all matters.
Seek out another leader – only they may be up to the task.
Though they live in different lands, Gilgamesh has found someone he can call ibru – friend.
Be in an Alliance with another Civilization.

The ox lies dazed in the palace courtyard, reeling from an unexpected punch. While war is always present, Gilgamesh desires to wrestle beasts and monsters, something that has concerned his livestock-keepers greatly.
Send patrols to find wonders and, perhaps, monsters of legend.
There have been no monsters, but Gilgamesh has become enthralled by the quest itself, poring over maps and planning new expeditions.
Construct a theater to depict epic battles from legend.

Gilgamesh’s palace is decorated with the trophies from legendary beasts: the feather of an anzu, the claw of a scorpion-man. But now, Gilgamesh hears of the Persian Immortals. He has already cleared a space on his wall for one of their shields.
The Immortal was, as it turns out, not.
Glory belongs to strategists, not would-be heroes.
As the library burns, tablets rain down from all sides, history smashing to dust on the stone floor. As the ashes cool, scribes gather what remains and leave them at the city temple.
The priests do their best to reconstruct what was lost.
The priests leave them as memorials to the dead.

Gilgamesh is a hero, not a general. He prefers his battles one-on-one, and his idea of kingship is of a shepherd governing a flock. But the Assyrian troops he commands call to him, asking him to take the battle-helmet up and speak to them from the ziggurat.
Deny them. Gilgamesh is a shepherd-king.
Give them what they want. Be the warrior-king.
He Was Given Knowledge Of Worship

Gilgamesh listens carefully to what his envoys report about the worship of the gods in foreign lands, and faces the altar. There, in clay, are the faces of the world’s creators – but to him, they are his kin.
Worship in the manner of others.
Another – ANOTHER – has completed what Gilgamesh sought to build. He spends his days at the construction pit, straining to place great stone bricks by hand. It is fruitless.
Gilgamesh will build some other thing.
Moody king Gilgamesh cannot keep his mind from the future. He gazes into a still bowl of water, demanding the gods show him some sign of what is to come. Eventually, a form takes shape.

Even when alone in the palace, Gilgamesh wonders what his ibru – his closest friend - is doing. Plotting strategic advances, he asks his general if his ally would do the same. Seeing a heavy boulder, he wonders if his ibru could lift it. Noticing a strong ox, he wonders if his ibru would like to see it wrestled. The attention has turned to obsession.

The diplomatic courier running between the two capitals is a known figure to the palace, waiting each morning for Gilgamesh’s message, then setting forth on the long journey to its destination. If only there was a similar courier delivering messages back.
With allies, support or have them support 5 Endeavors.
If there is one thing that Gilgamesh knows about friends, it is that they wrestle together. But with his ibru far away, he lacks inspiration.
Visitors marvel at Gilgamesh’s cities. Gilgamesh does not care – he waits only for one response.
Build and control a total of 3 Exploration Wonders.
The matters of state occupy Gilgamesh’s mind. He collects stories of military power from his commanders, then, in absentia. The greater the destruction, the better.
Send the king a story of a great fire.
The king leans forward to listen to the battler report, the light of the braziers glittering in his eyes. It is not the strategy he admires, it is the primal power in the flames.

Gilgamesh is horrified at the depictions of temples in far-off places. He hears of the gods - his kin - called the wrong names, worshipped in the wrong way. At night, his dreams are beset with the voices of his kin begging him to liberate them.
The gods have their proper name, and eat their proper food.
Capture a Holy City from another Civilization.

Tiamat’s fang. A lock of Humbaba’s beard. The Immortal’s shield. Gilgamesh gazes upon these and remembers the thrill of the clash. Now, he hears of Abbasid mamluks – the greatest cavalry, so it is said, in the world. And he thinks of yet another clash.
Horse armor would make a nice addition to the gallery.
The cry of battle, and the thud when the mamluk hit the ground! Gilgamesh imagines these and gazes at his gallery. The horse armor catches the light and glitters back redly.

Gilgamesh stares at himself in the mirror, combing oil into his beard, and brushing it over his biceps – then, his triceps, his pectoral muscles, his deltoids, his abdominal muscles. He stares again, approvingly. Then, a thought: “this other ruler,” he worries, “are they stronger still?”
Lats of iron. Abs of bronze. Gilgamesh dares his courtiers to bounce an ingot of high-quality iron off of his chest.
Stronger, perhaps. But never as handsome.
Gilgamesh grows tired of contests. He knows that his governance, his might, his beard surpass all others. What novelty, then, can the world have for him?
Take a holiday. He will still be the greatest king.
Others may strive. They are not demigods.

Have the most [icon:YIELD_DIPLOMACY] Influence per Turn for 10 more turns (non-consecutive). -2 [icon:YIELD_PRODUCTION] Production, [icon:YIELD_SCIENCE] Science, and [icon:YIELD_CULTURE] Culture in all Settlements during this quest.
Vigilance and diligence lead to greatness.
Ideologies are nothing compared to the clasp of an ibru’s hand. Yet Gilgamesh’s people seek an ideology, and they shall have one. But no philosophy book can transcend friendship.
Have exactly 1 Ally. Support or have that Ally Support 10 Endeavors. Getting more allies or losing this Ally ends the quest.
Hand in hand, Gilgamesh and his ibru face the world. As the flames of conflict rise, the love of a friend rises along with it. Victory or loss, this does not matter.
Have exactly 1 Ally. Support or have that Ally Support 10 Endeavors. Getting more allies or losing this Ally ends the quest.

There are no beasts. There are no monsters. In all the ages of the world, Gilgamesh has struggled to find a foe that can best his strength – but in the landship, it has arrived. Steel and smoke, iron and fire. A monster.
They are not dragons. They are not the anzu-bird. They are not the cypress-monster. But they are monsters, and they lie gutted and smoking on the battlefield.

Battles are not what they were. In the past, warriors would come at each other, their muscles straining, sweat pouring down their bodies as they grappled in the dust. Now, there is a crack, a plume of smoke, and a great man falls. But in that rifle report is the essence of death, and Gilgamesh will have it.
A sepoy’s musket is a mass-produced firearm; it is worn, its stock glossy from being passed from hand to hand over the years. It is not a marvel of engineering. But it represents victory.
Betrayal. A once-close friend of Gilgamesh has levied armies against him. The palace is full of the sound of crashing stone, breaking pottery. Betrayal. Gilgamesh cannot forget.
But he can forgive. Once the debt is paid.
